sec: Potassium Metabolism · physiology, compartments and electrophysiology

items.q: The opening line of the potassium page equates 1 mmol of K+ with which mass of potassium?
items.exp: The page prints 1 mmol K+ = 1 mEq K+ = 40 mg K+; 74.5 mg is the molecular weight of KCl, which the 750 mg tablet arithmetic on a later page uses. (Book p968)

items.q: Fill up: Total body potassium is computed on this page as ______ mEq per kilogram of body weight, giving about ______ mEq for the whole body.
items.exp: The formula is total body K+ = 50 mEq x body weight in kg, which the page works out as roughly 3000 mEq. (Book p968)

items.q: Assess the two intake figures on Book p968: I Daily potassium intake is stated as 4700 mg, about 100 mEq. II With the page's own formula, a 60 kg adult carries close to 3000 mEq of potassium.
items.exp: Both statements reproduce the page: 4700 mg daily intake is equated with about 100 mEq, and 50 mEq/kg x 60 kg is the 3000 mEq figure quoted. (Book p968)

items.q: Match each statement with the components column it comes from — 1) Serum potassium of 3.5 to 5.5 mEq/L 2) Potassium concentration of 100 to 125 mEq/L 3) 95 to 98% of total body potassium 4) Role in growth and in DNA and protein synthesis … A) ICF column B) ECF column
items.exp: Only the serum range 3.5-5.5 mEq/L belongs to the ECF column; the intracellular concentration, the 95-98% share and the anabolic role are all ICF entries. (Book p968)

items.q: A patient is given 40 mEq of potassium. By how much does this page expect the serum potassium to rise?
items.exp: The ECF column states that 40 mEq of supplementation raises serum K+ by only 0.5 mEq/L because most of it enters cells. (Book p968)

items.q: Every one of these appears in the ICF column of the components table EXCEPT:
opts: Supplementation raises the serum level by 0.5 mEq/L
It is the major intracellular cation
It helps in growth and in protein synthesis
items.exp: The blunted serum response to a 40 mEq load is an ECF-column statement; the other three, together with the 95-98% intracellular share, describe the ICF. (Book p968)

items.q: Match each compartment or organ with the potassium amount printed against it in the distribution table — 1) Muscle 2) Liver 3) Red blood cells 4) Plasma … A) 2650 mmol B) 250 mmol C) 350 mmol D) 15 mmol
items.exp: Muscle 2650, liver 250, interstitial fluid 35, red blood cells 350 and plasma 15 mmol are the five entries of the organ column. (Book p968)

items.q: Assess the distribution table on Book p968: I Its five organ values add to 3300 mmol although the total row reads 3000 mmol. II The compartment column gives 100 to 120 mmol/L for ICF and about 4 mmol/L for ECF.
items.exp: Both statements are literally correct, and they expose two source quirks: the organ entries overshoot the stated total, and the ICF concentration is 100-125 mEq/L in the components table but 100-120 mmol/L here. (Book p968)

items.q: A malnourished patient has a serum potassium of 2.3 mEq/L with generalized weakness and a silent abdomen. Which chain of events does this page's electrophysiology block use to explain those two findings?
opts: Fall in ECF K+ widens the gradient, K+ leaves the cell, the resting membrane potential becomes more negative and tissue excitability falls
Fall in ECF K+ narrows the gradient, K+ is retained, the resting potential becomes less negative and excitability rises
Rise in ECF K+ widens the gradient, K+ leaves the cell and the resting potential becomes more negative
Fall in ECF K+ widens the gradient, K+ leaves the cell, the resting potential becomes less negative and excitability rises
items.exp: The hypokalemia arrow runs from a low ECF or serum K+ through an increased outward gradient to a more negative resting membrane potential and reduced tissue excitability, which the page illustrates with muscle weakness and ileus. (Book p968)

items.q: All of the following are attached to the hypokalemia half of the electrophysiology block EXCEPT:
opts: A resting membrane potential that has become less negative
QT prolongation with torsades de pointes
items.exp: Low potassium makes the resting membrane potential more negative; a less negative potential is the hyperkalemia side of the same block, where tissue excitability rises and cardiac arrhythmias follow. (Book p968)

items.q: Fill up: In hyperkalemia the gradient for potassium to leave the cell is ______, so K+ ______ the cell, the resting membrane potential becomes ______ negative and tissue excitability ______.
items.exp: The hyperkalemia arrow describes a decreased outward gradient, potassium held inside the cell, a less negative resting potential and increased tissue excitability ending in cardiac arrhythmias. (Book p968)

items.q: Which cardiac rhythm complication does the page link to the increased cardiac excitability of hypokalemia?
opts: Torsades de pointes with QT prolongation
Atrial flutter with a short PR interval
Sinus bradycardia with a widened QRS
items.exp: The hypokalemia branch ends with increased cardiac excitability leading to torsades de pointes, annotated with QT prolongation. (Book p968)

items.q: An ECG in a patient with potassium 2.4 mEq/L shows a prolonged QT and runs of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia. Which two-step sequence from this page's block produced that picture?
opts: More negative resting potential with reduced tissue excitability, plus increased cardiac excitability
Less negative resting potential with increased tissue excitability, plus reduced cardiac excitability
More negative resting potential with increased tissue excitability in every tissue
Unchanged resting potential with selective skeletal muscle failure
items.exp: The page pairs a more negative resting potential with lowered tissue excitability for skeletal and gut muscle while simultaneously raising cardiac excitability, which is why weakness and torsades coexist. (Book p968)
